Indonesia's 1965-66 anti-communist purges are estimated to have killed 500,000 people or more.
The 1956 Suez Crisis exposed that Britain and France could no longer act as independent global powers without US backing, effectively closing their imperial era.
Aboard a Soviet submarine during the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis, officer Vasili Arkhipov's lone refusal to authorize a nuclear torpedo may have prevented a wider war.
Warsaw Pact forces, roughly 250,000 strong, crushed the reformist Prague Spring within months in 1968.
Mao's Great Leap Forward triggered a famine in 1958-1962 estimated to have killed tens of millions of people.
China's Cultural Revolution, launched in 1966, shut universities for years and sent millions of urban youth to labor in the countryside.
The Khmer Rouge's rule over Cambodia from 1975 to 1979 killed an estimated 1.5 to 2 million people, roughly a quarter of the population.
Louis XIV of France reigned for 72 years, the longest confirmed reign of any monarch in European history.
The Habsburgs expanded their realm largely through marriage, immortalized in the Latin motto: let others wage war; you, happy Austria, marry.
Elizabeth I of England never married, partly to avoid ceding power to a foreign husband, cultivating instead the image of the "Virgin Queen.
Beijing's Forbidden City, completed in 1420 under the Yongle Emperor, reportedly took roughly a million laborers to build.
Mughal emperor Akbar abolished the tax on non-Muslim subjects in 1564 and actively promoted religious tolerance, unusual for a 16th-century ruler.
Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal as a mausoleum for his favorite wife — then spent his final years imprisoned by the son who succeeded him.
Aurangzeb pushed the Mughal Empire to its largest territorial extent, but historians often blame his religious policies for accelerating its later decline.
At the Battle of Hastings in 1066, a feigned Norman retreat reportedly lured English soldiers out of their shield wall, breaking the line.
At Agincourt in 1415, a heavily outnumbered English army ravaged by dysentery still routed the French, largely thanks to the longbow.
Roughly 168 Spanish conquistadors captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca in 1532, despite facing an empire of millions.
The British East India Company won control of Bengal at the 1757 Battle of Plassey partly by bribing a rival commander to defect mid-battle.
British colonial forces suffered one of their worst defeats against a technologically inferior army at Isandlwana, Zulu territory, in 1879.
At Adwa in 1896, Ethiopian forces under Menelik II decisively defeated an invading Italian army, preserving Ethiopia's independence.
The 1916 Sykes-Picot Agreement secretly carved up the Ottoman Middle East between Britain and France, drawing lines that still shape conflicts today.
A British diplomat drew the Durand Line in 1893, splitting Pashtun territory between Afghanistan and British India — a border still disputed today.
The Treaty of Waitangi exists in English and Māori versions with subtly different meanings, a discrepancy still argued over in New Zealand courts.
The 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo forced Mexico to cede roughly half its territory to the United States, including present-day California and Arizona.
A secret protocol in the 1939 Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact divided Poland and the Baltic states between Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union before either invaded.
Peter the Great toured Western Europe incognito in the 1690s, working as a shipwright's apprentice in a Dutch shipyard to learn naval construction firsthand.
Simón Bolívar's campaigns helped liberate six modern South American countries from Spanish rule in the early 1800s.
Toussaint Louverture rose from slavery to lead the Haitian Revolution, negotiating with European powers before dying in a French prison in 1803.
Spartacus's slave rebellion defeated multiple Roman armies between 73 and 71 BC before its collapse; some 6,000 survivors were reportedly crucified along the Appian Way.
As a young man, Julius Caesar was captured by pirates — and after being ransomed, he hunted them down and had them crucified, just as he'd jokingly warned them he would.
Emperor Diocletian split Roman rule among four co-emperors in 293 AD, a system meant to stabilize the empire that instead triggered fresh civil wars.
Boudica led a revolt against Roman rule in Britain around 60-61 AD, reportedly burning the city of Londinium to the ground before her defeat.
Queen Zenobia of Palmyra briefly carved out an empire stretching into Egypt in the 3rd century AD before Rome's Aurelian defeated and reportedly paraded her in golden chains.
Empress Dowager Cixi effectively ruled China from behind a screen for nearly five decades in the late Qing dynasty.
Belgian colonial administrators issued identity cards labeling Rwandans and Burundians as Hutu or Tutsi, hardening categories that had once been far more fluid.
Britain fought the Opium Wars of 1839-1860 largely to keep selling opium into China, forcing Beijing to cede Hong Kong and open its ports to Western trade.
Foreign legations in Beijing endured a 55-day siege during the Boxer Rebellion of 1900 before an eight-nation relief force intervened.
Japan's 35-year annexation of Korea, beginning in 1910, included campaigns to suppress the Korean language in schools.
The Ottoman government's campaign against Armenians from 1915 to 1923 killed an estimated 1 to 1.5 million people — an event modern Turkey still disputes.
At Ain Jalut in 1260, the slave-soldier Mamluks of Egypt inflicted the first major defeat on a Mongol army, halting its advance into Africa.
Shah Ismail I made Twelver Shia Islam the official religion of Persia in 1501, a choice that still defines Iran's religious identity.
Archaeological evidence suggests Aboriginal Australians have maintained a continuous culture stretching back at least 65,000 years — the longest of any population on Earth.
Captain Cook charted much of the Pacific in the 1770s before being killed in Hawaii in 1779, in a dispute that began over a stolen ship's boat.
The Tu'i Tonga Empire projected influence across much of Polynesia through trade and tribute networks between roughly 1200 and 1500.
New Zealand was among the last major landmasses settled by humans, reached by Polynesian voyaging canoes only around 1250 to 1300 AD.
The Iroquois Confederacy united five, later six, Native nations under a shared council of representatives, a system with roots reaching back centuries before European contact.
The forced 1838 removal of the Cherokee and other nations, later called the Trail of Tears, killed thousands through exposure, disease and starvation along the way.
Some estimates suggest the 1864-1870 Paraguayan War killed more than half of Paraguay's population, including a staggering share of its adult men.
Hittite and Egyptian scribes recorded one of history's earliest known peace treaties after the Battle of Kadesh, around 1259 BC.
Ancient Nubian rulers at Meroë, in modern Sudan, built well over 200 pyramids — more than Egypt, though each considerably smaller.
According to tradition, the Phoenician queen Dido founded Carthage around 814 BC, a city that would grow to rival Rome for control of the western Mediterranean.
Mohenjo-daro, a city of the Indus Valley Civilization dating to around 2500 BC, had covered drains and household plumbing more advanced than many cities millennia later.
Chroniclers wrote that when the Mongols sacked Baghdad in 1258, so many books were dumped into the Tigris that the river ran black with ink.
London's Great Plague of 1665, a late outbreak of the same bacterium behind the Black Death, is estimated to have killed around 100,000 people.
The medieval Hanseatic League, a confederation of merchant cities, dominated Baltic and North Sea trade for centuries without ever becoming a formal state.
Modern experiments show fitted suits of medieval plate armor, at roughly 20-25 kg spread across the body, let a trained wearer run, climb and even roll on the ground.
Watergate's fallout made Richard Nixon, in 1974, the only US president ever to resign from office.
The US only formally acknowledged its role in the 1953 coup that toppled Iran's prime minister, Mohammad Mossadegh, decades after the fact.
The Marshall Plan funneled roughly $13 billion — well over $100 billion today — into rebuilding Western European economies after World War II.
Founded in 1961, the Non-Aligned Movement tried to chart a path for developing nations outside both the US and Soviet Cold War blocs.
Iran's 1979 revolution replaced a Western-backed monarchy with an Islamic republic in under a year.
The Berlin Wall's fall in 1989 was set off partly by a flustered East German spokesman who misspoke at a press conference, implying travel restrictions were lifted immediately.
The Rwandan genocide of 1994 killed an estimated 800,000 people, most of them Tutsi, in roughly 100 days.
China's civil war between Communists and Nationalists, fought from 1927 to 1949 with a wartime pause, ended with the Nationalist government's retreat to Taiwan.

The Mfecane, a period of upheaval and mass migration in early-19th-century southern Africa tied to Zulu expansion, reshaped the region's ethnic map and displaced groups thousands of kilometers from home.
The Kingdom of Dahomey, in what is now Benin, maintained an elite corps of female soldiers, sometimes called the Dahomey Amazons by European observers, well into the 19th century.
Aksum's King Ezana adopted Christianity as a state religion in the 4th century AD, decades before the Roman Empire did the same.
Vasco da Gama's 1498 voyage around Africa to India opened a direct sea route that let Portugal bypass centuries-old Venetian and Middle Eastern middlemen in the spice trade.
Cyclone Olivia struck Barrow Island, Australia in 1996 with a gust of 408 km/h — the fastest wind speed ever recorded on Earth's surface outside a tornado.
Before that gust was verified, Mount Washington in New Hampshire held the world wind speed record for 62 years, with a 1934 measurement of 372 km/h.
Georgia's Veryovkina Cave plunges roughly 2,209 metres into the Arabika Massif, making it the deepest known cave on Earth.
Malaysia's Sarawak Chamber is the largest known cave chamber by area — about 700 m long and 300 m wide, roomy enough to park dozens of jumbo jets.
Kentucky's Mammoth Cave has more than 686 km of mapped passages, about one and a half times longer than any other known cave system on Earth.
Vietnam's Hang Sơn Đoòng cave is so enormous it contains its own jungle, an underground river, and clouds that form near its ceiling.
Mexico's Naica Mine holds a chamber of gypsum crystals up to 12 metres long, grown over hundreds of thousands of years in mineral-rich water.
New Zealand's Waitomo Caves glow with thousands of bioluminescent glowworms whose silk threads mimic a starry night sky on the ceiling.
China's Three Gorges Dam holds so much water that NASA calculates it has slowed Earth's rotation by about 0.06 microseconds per day.
The 2004 Sumatra earthquake shifted enough mass to shorten Earth's day by an estimated 2.68 microseconds — over 40 times the effect of the Three Gorges Dam.
The 1960 Valdivia earthquake in Chile measured magnitude 9.5, the most powerful earthquake ever recorded by modern instruments.
The San Andreas Fault is slowly carrying Los Angeles toward San Francisco; at current rates, the two cities could sit side by side in roughly 15 million years.
The 1811-12 New Madrid earthquakes in the American Midwest were so violent that eyewitnesses reported the Mississippi River briefly appearing to flow backward.
Roughly 90% of the world's earthquakes and about three-quarters of its active volcanoes occur along the Pacific's so-called Ring of Fire.
Iceland's Laki volcano erupted for eight months in 1783, and the resulting sulfurous haze and famine are estimated to have killed a fifth of Iceland's population.
A Mexican farmer watched a volcano erupt straight out of his cornfield in 1943; within a year, Paricutin had grown into a cone over 300 metres tall.
Iceland's island of Surtsey rose from the sea in a 1963 eruption; scientists sealed it off immediately to study, untouched, how life colonizes new land.
Indonesia's Anak Krakatau, "Child of Krakatoa," grew from the original volcano's flooded crater starting in 1927, then partially collapsed in 2018, triggering a deadly tsunami.
Congo's Nyiragongo volcano holds one of Earth's few persistent lava lakes, and its unusually fluid lava can race downhill at up to 60 km/h.
Ethiopia's Erta Ale volcano has hosted a nearly continuous lava lake since at least 1906, earning it the nickname "Gateway to Hell.
Italy's Stromboli volcano has erupted in small bursts every 10 to 20 minutes for roughly 2,000 years, earning it sailors' nickname "Lighthouse of the Mediterranean.
A vent on Hawaii's Kilauea, Puʻu ʻŌʻō, erupted almost continuously from 1983 to 2018, 35 years of nearly unbroken activity.
Antarctica's Mount Erebus is one of the only volcanoes on Earth with a long-lived lava lake, bubbling away in one of the coldest places on the planet.
Straddling Chile and Argentina, Ojos del Salado rises to roughly 6,893 m, making it the highest volcano on Earth — and it still occasionally steams.
Yellowstone's caldera, carved out by a supereruption 640,000 years ago, spans roughly 50 by 70 km; visitors drive across it without ever noticing.
Sumatra's Lake Toba fills the crater of a supervolcano that erupted an estimated 2,800 cubic km of material about 74,000 years ago, one of the largest eruptions in recent geological history.
India's Deccan Traps, a volcanic plateau covering roughly half a million square km, erupted around the time the dinosaurs went extinct 66 million years ago.
Siberia's Traps eruptions some 252 million years ago covered an area nearly the size of Australia and are linked to the worst mass extinction in Earth's history.
Djibouti's Lake Assal sits about 155 m below sea level, the lowest point in Africa, and its water runs close to 35% salt — saltier than the Dead Sea.
Western Australia's Lake Hillier is a permanent, vivid bubblegum pink, a color that persists even when the water is scooped into a bottle.
Senegal's Lake Retba turns rose-pink in the dry season thanks to salt-loving algae, and villagers have harvested salt from its shallows for generations.
Africa's Lake Malawi is home to an estimated 700 to 1,000 species of cichlid fish, more than any other lake on Earth.
Lake Tanganyika is the world's second-deepest and second-oldest lake, formed in the East African Rift an estimated 9 to 12 million years ago.
Oregon's Crater Lake formed when Mount Mazama collapsed about 7,700 years ago; at nearly 594 m deep, it's the deepest lake in the United States.
Lake Chad has shrunk by more than 90% since the 1960s, squeezed by drought, shifting climate and rising water demand.
Antarctica's Lake Vanda stays sealed under ice all year, yet its bottom waters can reach around 25°C, warmed by trapped sunlight and geothermal heat.
Ethiopia's Danakil Depression averages annual highs above 41°C, making it widely considered the hottest continuously inhabited place on Earth.
A hailstone that fell near Vivian, South Dakota in 2010 measured about 20 cm across and weighed nearly 0.9 kg, the largest ever recovered in the US.
Washington's Mount Baker Ski Area logged 1,140 inches, about 29 metres, of snow in the winter of 1998-99, a world record for snowfall in a single season.
A lightning bolt recorded over Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi in April 2020 stretched roughly 768 km, the longest single flash ever certified.
A storm over Uruguay and Argentina in June 2020 produced a single lightning flash lasting 17.1 seconds, the longest duration ever recorded.
Venezuela's Lake Maracaibo sees so-called Catatumbo lightning on an estimated 140 to 160 nights a year, making it one of the most lightning-dense spots on Earth.
The Amazon River has no bridges anywhere along its roughly 6,400 km length — its banks are simply too remote and its channel too wide.
Near Manaus, Brazil, the dark Rio Negro and the pale, sandy Amazon run side by side for kilometres without fully mixing, thanks to differences in temperature, speed and density.
Brazil's Iguazu Falls is made up of some 275 individual cascades spread across nearly 3 km, wider than either Niagara or Victoria Falls.
China's Qiantang River produces the world's largest tidal bore, sending walls of water up to 9 m high surging upstream against the current.
The Ganges-Brahmaputra Delta, spanning Bangladesh and eastern India, is the largest river delta on Earth, built from sediment carried down from the Himalayas.
Siberia's Lena River empties into a delta so vast and cold that it stays frozen for more than half the year, forming one of the world's largest protected wetlands.
Seasonal floods can raise the Amazon's water level by as much as 10 m, submerging riverside forest so completely that fish swim between the tree trunks.
Antarctica hides more than 400 known subglacial lakes of liquid water, kept unfrozen by geothermal heat trapped beneath kilometres of ice.
Namibia's Namib Desert is thought to be the oldest desert on Earth, with arid conditions persisting for an estimated 55 to 80 million years.
Arabia's Rub' al Khali, or Empty Quarter, is the largest continuous sand desert on Earth, covering an area bigger than France.
Mongolia's Gobi Desert gets cold enough to snow in winter and has yielded some of the richest dinosaur fossil beds ever found, including the Flaming Cliffs.
Shifting dunes in China's Taklamakan Desert have swallowed entire ancient cities; its name is often said to mean "go in and you won't come out.
Antarctica's McMurdo Dry Valleys are so parched that some soils there haven't seen rain in millions of years, and mummified seal carcasses can be centuries old.
New Zealand's landmass is just the visible tip of Zealandia, a mostly submerged continent roughly 94% underwater.
Yemen's Socotra island has been isolated so long that an estimated third of its plant species, including the umbrella-shaped dragon's blood tree, grow nowhere else on Earth.
Green turtles migrate more than 2,000 km from feeding grounds off Brazil to nest on the beaches of remote, volcanic Ascension Island.
Norway's Bouvet Island, a volcanic speck in the South Atlantic, is considered the most remote island on Earth, with Antarctica its nearest land some 1,700 km away.
Canada's Baffin Island, the world's fifth-largest island, covers more area than Sweden.
Ellesmere Island lies so far north its coasts brush the Arctic Ocean's permanent ice, yet muskoxen still graze there year-round.
Japan's Iwo Jima has risen several metres out of the Pacific over the past century, pushed upward by the same volcanic activity that formed it.

The Wallace Line, an invisible boundary running through the Indonesian archipelago, separates islands with Asian-descended mammals from islands with marsupials and other Australian-descended wildlife.
Isolation drove Galápagos finches on different islands to evolve distinctly shaped beaks, observations that helped shape Darwin's theory of evolution.

Baobab trees grow wild in Africa, Madagascar and Australia — continents that split apart tens of millions of years before botanists think their seeds could have crossed by ocean current, a puzzle still debated today.
The boreal forest, or taiga, stretching across Russia, Scandinavia and Canada, is the largest land biome on Earth, holding roughly a third of the world's forest cover.
Australia's Daintree Rainforest is estimated to be around 180 million years old, making it older than flowering plants themselves.
Roughly 1.2 to 2 million wildebeest migrate in a continuous loop across the Serengeti and Maasai Mara each year, chasing the rains.
Arctic terns fly an estimated 70,000 km round trip between the Arctic and Antarctic every year, farther than any other migrating animal.
In 2022, satellite tracking showed a bar-tailed godwit flying 13,560 km nonstop from Alaska to Tasmania without landing once, the longest known nonstop bird flight.
Monarch butterflies that have never made the trip before still navigate up to 4,500 km from Canada and the US to the same patch of Mexican fir forest their ancestors used.
Lake Baikal is home to the nerpa, the world's only exclusively freshwater seal species, living roughly 1,600 km from the nearest ocean.
Mangroves are among the only trees able to survive rooted in saltwater, forming coastal buffers across some 118 countries in the tropics and subtropics.
Permafrost underlies roughly a quarter of the land in the Northern Hemisphere, locking away carbon that has been accumulating for thousands of years.
The Denmark Strait cataract, an underwater waterfall formed where cold and warm water masses collide between Greenland and Iceland, drops roughly 3,500 m — taller than any waterfall on land.
South Africa's Agulhas Current can generate rogue waves so steep that ships have reported nearly being swallowed whole in otherwise ordinary seas.
The 1995 "Draupner wave," a 25.6 m rogue wave recorded in the North Sea, was the first scientific measurement to confirm freak waves were real, not sailors' exaggeration.
Cold, nutrient-rich water from the Humboldt Current makes the seas off Peru and Chile some of the most productive fisheries on Earth, until El Niño disrupts the flow.
Deep-sea "black smokers," hydrothermal vents first found in 1977, host thriving ecosystems that run on chemical energy instead of sunlight.
Giant kelp can grow up to 60 cm in a single day, making it one of the fastest-growing organisms on the planet.
The ocean's so-called twilight zone, roughly 200 to 1,000 m down, is estimated to hold more fish biomass than every other part of the ocean combined.
Southeast Asia's Coral Triangle holds an estimated 76% of the world's known coral species within less than 2% of the ocean's area.
Puerto Rico's Mosquito Bay glows blue-green at night from densely packed bioluminescent plankton, making it one of the brightest bioluminescent bays on Earth.
Greenland's Scoresby Sund is the longest fjord system in the world, reaching more than 350 km inland from the coast.
Argentina's Perito Moreno Glacier is one of the few glaciers on Earth still advancing rather than retreating, occasionally damming an entire lake before collapsing.
Greenland's Jakobshavn Glacier reached speeds of about 46 m a day in 2012, among the fastest glacier flows ever measured.
Antarctica's Lambert Glacier stretches more than 400 km and, with its ice shelf, drains an estimated 16% of the entire East Antarctic ice sheet.
Iceland's Vatnajökull is Europe's largest ice cap by volume, covering roughly 8% of the country's land area.
On New Zealand's South Island, the Franz Josef and Fox glaciers descend almost to sea level, spilling into temperate rainforest just kilometres from the coast.
Ethiopia's Afar Triangle is one of the few places on Earth where a mid-ocean ridge, normally hidden under the sea, is exposed on dry land.
At Iceland's Þingvellir, visitors can walk, or even dive, through a rift where the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates are pulling apart a few centimetres a year.
East Africa's rift valley is slowly tearing the continent in two; geologists expect a new ocean will eventually flood the gap, tens of millions of years from now.
India was once a separate landmass that drifted roughly 6,000 km north before colliding with Asia, a slow-motion crash that still pushes the Himalayas higher today.
The Democratic Republic of Congo mines an estimated 70% or more of the world's cobalt, a metal now essential to rechargeable batteries.
Chile holds roughly a quarter of the world's known copper reserves and remains the top copper-producing country on Earth.
Saudi Arabia's Ghawar Field, discovered in 1948, is the largest conventional oil field ever found and has produced tens of billions of barrels since 1951.
The Ogallala Aquifer stretches beneath eight US Great Plains states and irrigates a huge share of American farmland, even as it's pumped faster than rain can refill it.
Tanzania's Ol Doinyo Lengai is the only volcano on Earth known to erupt natrocarbonatite lava, a strange black flow that turns chalky white within hours of cooling.
Venezuela's Mount Roraima is a flat-topped tepui with sheer cliffs up to 400 m tall, its isolated summit plateau said to have inspired Arthur Conan Doyle's "The Lost World.
Table Mountain in Cape Town is estimated at around 260 million years old, making it far older than the Atlantic Ocean it now overlooks.
Indonesia's Puncak Jaya carries small equatorial glaciers above 4,800 m, among the very few glaciers found near the equator anywhere on Earth.
Tibet's Mount Kailash has never been officially climbed; it's sacred to four religions, and expeditions have historically avoided its summit out of respect.
Antarctica's Vinson Massif, the continent's highest peak at around 4,892 m, wasn't climbed until 1966, decades after Everest.
France and Italy's Concordia Station, perched on Antarctica's Dome C, recorded -84.7°C in 2010 — the coldest temperature ever measured outside Vostok Station.
Satellite data has recorded surface temperatures as low as an estimated -93°C on the East Antarctic Plateau, colder than any thermometer has confirmed on the ground.
Australia's Great Artesian Basin, one of the largest underground water reservoirs on Earth, lies beneath nearly a fifth of the continent and can push water to the surface under its own pressure.

Peru's Boiling River in the Amazon runs at nearly 95°C on average, with hot springs feeding it recorded above 99°C — hot enough to kill animals that fall in, despite no volcano for hundreds of kilometres.
Yellowstone's Grand Prismatic Spring owes its rainbow colors to heat-loving bacteria that shift by temperature zone, from orange at the cooler edges to deep blue at its boiling center.
Turkey's Pamukkale, meaning "cotton castle," is a hillside of white travertine terraces built up over thousands of years by cascading mineral-rich hot springs.
Australia's Simpson Desert holds sand dunes that run parallel for hundreds of kilometres, among the most regular dune fields on Earth.
Namibia's Dune 7, near Walvis Bay, rises roughly 383 m, making it one of the tallest sand dunes on Earth.
Papua New Guinea covers well under 1% of Earth's land surface, yet its rainforests are estimated to hold around 5% of the world's known species.
The Democratic Republic of Congo's rainforest is the second-largest contiguous rainforest on Earth after the Amazon, spanning roughly 2 million square km.
Borneo's rainforests, in continuous existence for over 100 million years, host thousands of species found nowhere else, including orangutans.
New Zealand had no native land mammals besides bats before humans arrived, leaving birds like the kiwi to fill ecological roles mammals play elsewhere.
Australia is the only continent naturally home to monotremes, the egg-laying mammals like the platypus and echidna, a lineage found nowhere else on Earth.
Nearly all of Madagascar's roughly 100 lemur species descend from a single ancestral population, since lemurs are the only primate lineage ever to reach the island.
The Galápagos marine iguana is the only lizard on Earth known to forage in the ocean, diving to graze on algae along the seafloor.
Antarctica's only two native flowering plants survive on an otherwise plant-free continent, clinging to a narrow ice-free strip of the Antarctic Peninsula.
Antarctic icefish are the only vertebrates known to lack both red blood cells and hemoglobin, surviving instead on oxygen dissolved directly in frigid, oxygen-rich water.
Emperor penguins are the only animal known to breed through the depths of the Antarctic winter, incubating eggs on their feet in temperatures below -40°C.
Ice flow carries survey markers placed near the geographic South Pole roughly 10 m a year, meaning the exact marked spot has already shifted by the following season.
Point Barrow, Alaska sits farther north than the northernmost tip of Russia's mainland, making it the northernmost point of the United States.
Argentina's Ushuaia, often billed the world's southernmost city, still sits more than 3,000 km from the South Pole — a reminder of how vast the journey to Antarctica remains.
Svalbard's Longyearbyen, one of the world's northernmost towns, goes without direct sunlight for about four months every winter.
Chile's Villa Las Estrellas and Argentina's Base Esperanza are among the only settlements in Antarctica with permanent residents, including families and a school.
Nunavut's Alert sits just 817 km from the North Pole, making it the northernmost permanently inhabited place on Earth.
Palmyra Atoll, a US territory in the central Pacific, has no permanent human residents but hosts one of the most pristine coral reef ecosystems left on Earth.
Morocco's Erg Chebbi dunes rise more than 150 m in the Sahara, though they're dwarfed by Namibia's Dune 7 farther south.
The Volga is Europe's longest river at roughly 3,530 km, flowing entirely within Russia before draining into the landlocked Caspian Sea.
The Yukon River flows more than 3,000 km through both Canada and Alaska before reaching the Bering Sea, one of North America's longest rivers.
Unlike most rivers that flow toward warmer latitudes, the Nile runs north for more than 6,000 km from its highland sources to the Mediterranean.
The Zambezi's roughly 2,700 km course to the Indian Ocean includes more than 70 rapids and waterfalls, among them Victoria Falls partway down.
Papua New Guinea's Sepik River winds so extensively through swampy lowlands that its straight-line length is barely a third of its actual, meandering course.
Siberia's Ob River system drains an area larger than India into the Arctic Ocean through the Gulf of Ob.
China's Yellow River carries so much silt that its delta has gained an average of about 22 square km of new land a year since shifting course into the Bohai Sea in 1855.
South Sudan's Sudd wetland, formed where the White Nile spreads across a vast flat plain, swells from around 30,000 to more than 130,000 square km in the rainy season.
Brazil's Pantanal is the largest tropical wetland on Earth, covering an estimated 140,000 to 195,000 square km across Brazil, Bolivia and Paraguay.
Florida's Everglades is technically a slow-moving river some 100 km wide but often just centimetres deep, long nicknamed a "river of grass.
Only about 1% of Scotland's original Caledonian pine forest survives today, reduced from roughly 1.5 million hectares to scattered remnants covering under 20,000 hectares.
Chile's temperate rainforests along the Pacific coast of Patagonia rank among the wettest ecosystems outside the tropics, with more than 5 metres of rain a year in places.
Australia holds an estimated third of the world's known uranium reserves, more than any other country.
Chile, Argentina and Bolivia's shared salt flats hold such rich lithium brine deposits that the region is nicknamed the "Lithium Triangle.
Decades of phosphate mining stripped from its own guano deposits left much of the small Pacific island of Nauru's interior a barren, cratered moonscape.
Iceland sits directly atop the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, one of the only places on Earth where new ocean crust is built up above sea level rather than hidden beneath it.
Kenya's Lake Turkana is the world's largest permanent desert lake, sitting in one of the hottest, most arid corners of East Africa.
Brazil's Carajás mining complex sits atop one of the largest iron ore deposits on Earth, carved from rainforest in the eastern Amazon.
Chile's Escondida mine, high in the Atacama, is the largest copper mine on Earth by output, alone supplying a meaningful share of global demand.
Australia's Pilbara region supplies more than half the world's seaborne iron ore trade, shipped from some of the planet's oldest exposed rock.
Canada's Hudson Bay Lowlands form the world's second-largest peatland complex, storing an estimated 30 to 39 billion tonnes of carbon across roughly 372,000 square km.
India overtook China as the world's most populous country in 2023; by 2026 it counts roughly 1.48 billion people to China's 1.41 billion, per UN projections.
Monaco's median age is around 55, the oldest of any country on Earth. Niger's is under 15 — the two extremes of the human age spectrum.
Bulgaria's population has been shrinking faster than almost any other country's this century, driven by low birth rates and decades of emigration.
China's one-child policy, enforced from 1980 to 2015, is estimated to have prevented several hundred million births — and left the country with a shrinking workforce today.
Israel's fertility rate, near 3 births per woman, is the highest in the OECD by a wide margin; most wealthy countries now sit below 1.5.
The United Arab Emirates' population is estimated to be roughly 90% foreign residents, one of the highest expatriate shares of any country on Earth.
Around 2018, people aged 65 and older outnumbered children under 5 worldwide for the first time in recorded history — and the gap has widened every year since.
Puerto Rico's population has fallen by more than 10% since 2010 through emigration and low birth rates, one of the sharpest peacetime declines on record.
Italy's population has shrunk every year since 2014; without sustained immigration, some forecasts see it losing millions more residents by the 2050s.
Roughly 1 in 8 people worldwide is over 60 today. The UN expects that to be closer to 1 in 6 by 2050.
India's population is markedly younger than China's — a median age near 29 versus roughly 40 — a demographic edge economists watch closely.
Nigeria is projected to become the world's third most populous country by 2050, overtaking the United States, per UN projections.
Qatar's population is over 2.5 million, yet fewer than 1 in 10 residents hold Qatari citizenship — nearly everyone else is a foreign worker.
By the end of 2025, an estimated 117.8 million people worldwide were forcibly displaced by conflict or persecution — more than 1 in every 70 people on Earth, per UNHCR.
Turkey has hosted more refugees than any other country for over a decade, sheltering more than 3 million Syrians alone.
Germany's postwar "Gastarbeiter" program brought in millions of guest workers, mostly from Turkey, starting in the 1950s — many stayed and reshaped the country's population.
More people of Lebanese descent are estimated to live outside Lebanon than inside it, a diaspora built over more than a century of emigration.
Armenia's diaspora is estimated to be several times larger than Armenia's own population, spread across Russia, France, the US and beyond.
Ireland's diaspora is estimated at tens of millions worldwide, a figure many times the roughly 5 million people who live on the island today.
Qatar and the UAE draw so much of their labor force from South Asia that Indian, Pakistani, Bangladeshi and Nepali nationals together outnumber local citizens.
Britain's 1948-1971 "Windrush generation" brought tens of thousands of Caribbean migrants to help rebuild postwar Britain; many only had their citizenship formally confirmed decades later.
The US-Mexico corridor is one of the largest remittance routes on Earth, moving tens of billions of dollars a year from migrant workers to families back home.
Europe saw over a million asylum applications in a single year at least twice in the past decade, its largest forced movement of people since World War Two.
About 30% of Australia's population was born overseas, one of the highest shares among large developed economies.
Canada admits several hundred thousand new permanent residents a year, a rate that, relative to population, far exceeds the United States'.
Nepal's economy leans so heavily on migrant labor abroad that remittances are estimated to equal roughly a quarter of the country's entire GDP.
Japan, long closed to large-scale immigration, has quietly become one of Asia's top destinations for migrant workers as its aging economy runs short of labor.
Lagos has grown from roughly 1 million people in 1970 to an estimated 15 million or more today, making it one of the fastest-growing megacities on Earth.
Shenzhen was a fishing town of about 30,000 people in 1980. Designated a special economic zone that year, it now holds more than 17 million.
Delhi's metro area is growing so fast the UN projects it could become the world's single most populous urban agglomeration within a couple of decades.
An estimated 1 billion people worldwide live in informal settlements or slums, most in rapidly urbanizing cities across Africa and Asia.
Singapore has expanded its land area by roughly a quarter since independence in 1965, almost entirely through land reclamation.
Residency in Pyongyang is tightly restricted by the North Korean state — living in the capital is treated as a privilege, not a right.
Detroit's population has fallen by more than half since its 1950s peak of roughly 1.85 million, one of the steepest declines of any major Western city.
The number of "megacities" with over 10 million people has grown from about 10 in 1990 to more than 30 today, per UN data.
Mumbai's Dharavi packs an estimated 1 million or more residents into roughly 2 square kilometres, among the densest urban patches on Earth.
Brasília was built from nothing in under four years and became Brazil's capital in 1960, its master plan laid out in the shape of an airplane.
Nearly 40% of Egypt's population is squeezed into greater Cairo and the Nile Delta, leaving most of the country's land area almost empty.
Ho Chi Minh City's population has roughly quadrupled since Vietnam's post-1986 economic reforms sent rural migrants pouring into its factories and service jobs.
There are more than 300 distinct sign languages in use worldwide — they are not one universal language, and most aren't mutually intelligible.
English is estimated to have borrowed roughly 80% of its vocabulary from other languages, chiefly Latin, French and Greek.
Louis Braille invented his raised-dot reading system in the 1820s at age 15, after losing his sight in a childhood accident.
Cyrillic script, developed in the 9th century, is now used to write more than 50 languages across Eastern Europe and Central Asia.
Silbo Gomero, a whistled language used on Spain's La Gomera island, can carry conversations across valleys several kilometres apart.
Duolingo reports several hundred million registered users worldwide, making a phone app one of the largest informal language-learning tools in history.
Literate adults need to recognize roughly 3,000 to 4,000 Chinese characters for basic newspaper fluency, far more than any alphabet requires.
Esperanto, invented in 1887 to be a universal second language, is estimated to have at most a few hundred thousand fluent speakers today.
Speakers of Spanish, Italian and Portuguese share enough vocabulary that they can often follow one another's news broadcasts without ever studying the other language.
UNESCO estimates more than 40% of the roughly 7,000 languages spoken today are at risk of disappearing within a few generations.
Devanagari script and its relatives are used to write dozens of modern Indian languages, from Hindi and Marathi to Nepali.
Arabic script, adapted for languages from Persian to Urdu to Malay, is used by far more people than the Arabic language itself.
Vietnamese was written in Chinese-derived characters for centuries before French colonial rule pushed it toward the Latin-based alphabet used today.
Christianity and Islam together account for over half of humanity, with roughly 2.4 billion and 2 billion adherents respectively by recent estimates.
The religiously unaffiliated number over a billion people worldwide, yet their global population share is projected to shrink as affiliated groups post higher birth rates.
Mecca's Hajj draws an estimated 1.5 to 2 million Muslims a year, one of the largest annual gatherings of humanity in one place.
The world's Jewish population, estimated at roughly 15-16 million today, has still not recovered to its pre-Holocaust level of about 16.5 million in 1939.
Zoroastrianism, once the state religion of the Persian Empire, is estimated to have fewer than 200,000 adherents left worldwide.
Sikhism, founded in 15th-century Punjab, now counts an estimated 25-30 million adherents, most still concentrated in that one Indian region.
Jainism has only a few million followers, almost all in India, yet its doctrine of nonviolence has shaped Indian vegetarianism far beyond its numbers.
Japan has more Shinto shrines than convenience stores, tens of thousands of them scattered across the country, many tiny and unstaffed.
Ethiopia's Orthodox Christian and Muslim communities have coexisted for well over a thousand years, since Islam arrived within the Prophet Muhammad's own lifetime.
Bahrain's population includes a Shia Muslim majority ruled by a Sunni royal family, a religious imbalance that has shaped decades of domestic tension.
Mauritius is one of the few countries outside South Asia where Hindus form the largest religious group, a legacy of 19th-century indentured labor migration.
The Amish population in the United States has roughly doubled every 20 years for decades, driven almost entirely by large families rather than conversion.
El Salvador made bitcoin legal tender in 2021, then reversed the mandate in 2025 under IMF pressure — it remains the only country to have tried it.
The Hong Kong dollar has been pegged at roughly 7.8 to the US dollar since 1983, one of the longest-running currency pegs on Earth.
Zimbabwe introduced its sixth new currency in 15 years in April 2024, a gold-backed unit called the ZiG, after its previous dollar collapsed on the black market.
Fourteen African countries still use the CFA franc, a currency pegged to the euro and historically guaranteed by the French treasury, an arrangement dating to the colonial era.
The United States holds the world's largest official gold reserves, at more than 8,000 tonnes, more than the next several countries combined.
Japan's public debt runs to roughly 235% of GDP, among the highest of any large economy, yet its borrowing costs stayed historically low for decades.
Panama, Liberia and the Marshall Islands together fly the flags of over 40% of the world's cargo shipping capacity, despite owning almost none of the ships themselves.
Grameen Bank, founded in Bangladesh in 1983, pioneered microloans of just a few dollars and helped launch a global microfinance industry.
Roughly 79% of adults worldwide now have a bank or mobile-money account, per World Bank Findex data, up sharply in just a few years — though hundreds of millions remain unbanked.
Cash is estimated to make up only a small single-digit share of retail payments in Sweden, one of the most cashless societies on Earth.
Taiwan's TSMC alone makes an estimated 70% of the world's outsourced advanced computer chips, giving one company outsized leverage over the global economy.
Nauru briefly became one of the richest countries per capita in the 1970s from phosphate mining, then faced near-bankruptcy within a generation once the reserves ran out.
Somalia's economy runs heavily on informal remittance networks known as hawala, since much of the country lacks a functioning conventional banking system.
China produces more than half the world's steel, more than every other producing country combined.
Roughly 1.3 million kilometres of undersea fiber-optic cable now carry the vast majority of intercontinental internet traffic, not satellites.
China's high-speed rail network grew from almost nothing in 2008 to over 45,000 km of track today, more than the rest of the world's high-speed lines combined.
An estimated 730 million people worldwide still lacked access to electricity in 2024, according to the IEA, with Sub-Saharan Africa accounting for roughly 8 in 10 of them.
China's Three Gorges Dam generates more electricity in a year than some entire mid-sized countries consume.
Rare earth elements essential to electronics and green technology are overwhelmingly refined in China, even when they're mined elsewhere.
The Öresund link between Denmark and Sweden, opened in 2000, was among the first structures to connect two countries by both road and rail over open water.
Continental Europe runs one of the largest synchronized electricity grids on Earth, linking the power systems of more than 25 countries.
India's state railway employs well over a million people directly, making it one of the largest single employers on the planet.
China's Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge, the world's longest, stretches roughly 165 km, built mostly over rice paddies and lakes for a high-speed rail line.
Global cement production has roughly quadrupled since 1990, with China alone responsible for more than half of it.
Roughly 2.2 billion people worldwide lack safely managed drinking water at home, per WHO and UNICEF — more than 1 in 4 of all humanity.
Dubai's Jebel Ali Port grew from empty desert in the 1970s into one of the largest man-made harbors on Earth.
Shanghai's port moved more than 51 million shipping containers in 2024, more than any other port on Earth by a wide margin.
Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson airport has ranked among the world's busiest for years, handling well over 100 million passengers annually.
Shanghai's two airports combined handled roughly 135 million passengers in a recent year, overtaking Tokyo as Asia's busiest airport city.
The world's commercial airline fleet has grown to more than 25,000 aircraft, moving billions of passengers a year in an industry that barely existed a century ago.
India's rail network carries more than 20 million passengers on an average day, roughly the population of a mid-sized country, every single day.
The Netherlands has more bicycles than people, and cycling accounts for a larger share of everyday trips there than almost anywhere else on Earth.
Container shipping is estimated to move roughly 80% or more of world trade by volume, almost entirely invisible to the people who buy what's inside.
The Strait of Hormuz, only about 33 km wide at its narrowest, is the transit route for roughly a fifth of the world's oil supply.
Ethiopian Airlines has grown into Africa's largest carrier, linking the continent to Asia and the Middle East through its Addis Ababa hub.
Mumbai's suburban railway carries several million riders a day at densities that make it one of the most crowded transit systems on Earth.
The Beijing-Shanghai high-speed line covers roughly 1,300 km in under five hours, a trip that once took a full day or more by conventional rail.
Air cargo carries only a small fraction of world trade by weight but an estimated third or more of it by value, mostly electronics, medicine and perishables.
The world's registered merchant fleet now carries far more total cargo tonnage than a generation ago, even as crews have gotten smaller and ships larger.
Nearly 138 million children were engaged in child labor worldwide in 2024, almost two-thirds of them in Sub-Saharan Africa, per ILO and UNICEF estimates.
An estimated 50 million people worldwide were living in modern slavery as of 2021 — forced labor or forced marriage — according to the ILO, Walk Free and IOM.
More than 60% of the world's workers are estimated to hold informal jobs with no contract, benefits or legal protection, concentrated heavily in developing economies.
Women's labor-force participation in parts of the Middle East and North Africa remains below 25%, among the lowest rates of any region on Earth.

Retirement ages range from under 60 in some countries to 67 or higher in others, often for populations with very different life expectancies.
The United States is one of the only wealthy countries with no federal law guaranteeing paid parental leave.
Union membership in Nordic countries can exceed 60-70% of the workforce, compared with roughly 1 in 10 workers in the United States.
Youth unemployment has topped 30% in parts of Southern Europe and North Africa in recent years, even as employers elsewhere report labor shortages.
The "kafala" sponsorship system, used across much of the Gulf for decades, ties a migrant worker's legal status directly to a single employer.
Informal domestic work, largely performed by women, is estimated to employ tens of millions of people worldwide with little to no legal protection in most countries.
Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a global vaccination campaign, the only human disease ever wiped out entirely.

Nauru has one of the highest smoking rates on Earth, with nearly half its adult population using tobacco, per recent estimates.

Antibiotic-resistant infections are estimated to contribute to more than a million deaths a year worldwide, a toll health officials warn is still rising.
Blood type distribution varies sharply by region: type O dominates across much of the Americas, while type B is far more common in parts of Central and South Asia.
South Korea has one of the highest rates of cosmetic surgery per capita on Earth, with a large share of young adults reporting having had a procedure.

Surgical care remains out of reach for an estimated 5 billion people worldwide, mostly in low- and middle-income countries, according to global health researchers.
Life expectancy for women exceeds that of men in nearly every country on Earth, typically by 4 to 7 years, though the exact causes are still debated.
Diabetes prevalence has risen fastest across the Pacific islands and parts of the Gulf, some of which now report adult rates above 20%.
Roughly a third of all food produced worldwide is lost or wasted every year, from farm to fork, per UN Environment Programme estimates.
Between 638 and 720 million people faced hunger in 2024, with Africa alone accounting for over 300 million of them, per the UN's latest food security report.
Just three crops — wheat, rice and maize — supply roughly half of all the calories humans consume worldwide.
Colombia, Vietnam and Brazil together grow a large share of the world's coffee, feeding a global market worth tens of billions of dollars a year.
Indonesia and Malaysia together produce the overwhelming majority of the world's palm oil, now found in roughly half of packaged supermarket products.
Brazil and India together account for a large share of the world's cane sugar production.
France, Italy and Spain together produce roughly half the world's wine by volume, a share that has slipped as vineyards spread to new countries.
China now produces more honey than any other country, much of it moving through export markets rather than domestic tables.
Overfishing has pushed roughly a third of the world's monitored fish stocks beyond biologically sustainable limits, per UN fisheries assessments.

Russia, the US, Canada, France and Australia together account for the majority of the world's wheat traded across borders.

Smartphone ownership has passed 90% of adults in much of East Asia and Europe, while parts of Sub-Saharan Africa remain below half, per recent global surveys.
Solar power has become the cheapest source of new electricity in most of the world, a reversal from a decade ago when it was among the most expensive options.
More than 40 countries have now launched their own satellites, though a handful of spacefaring nations still account for the vast majority of orbital launches.
Satellite-internet services like Starlink have begun reaching rural communities that traditional telecom companies never found profitable to wire.
Social media penetration exceeds 80% of the population in several wealthy and middle-income countries alike, narrowing older gaps in internet access.
E-commerce accounts for a larger share of retail spending in China than in almost any other major economy, built around mobile-payment platforms.
5G rollout has moved fastest across East Asia and the Gulf states, while much of the world still runs primarily on 4G or older networks.

Telemedicine consultations surged worldwide during the COVID-19 pandemic and have stayed far above pre-pandemic levels in many countries since.

Azerbaijan's Nakhchivan region is cut off from the rest of the country by Armenian territory, yet it still borders both Iran and Turkey.

Point Roberts, Washington, sits on a peninsula tip so oddly placed that reaching the rest of the United States by road means driving through Canada first.

Gibraltar's airport runway crosses its own main road; traffic barriers close whenever a plane needs to land or take off from the British territory.
Spain still garrisons a handful of tiny islets off Morocco's Mediterranean coast, some barely larger than a football pitch, claimed as sovereign Spanish soil.
Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten are constituent countries of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, sitting in the Caribbean thousands of kilometres from Amsterdam.
France's overseas department of French Guiana, on South America's northern coast, is legally as much a part of France as Paris — giving the EU a land border with Brazil.
Greenland voted to leave the European Communities in 1985, decades before Brexit, even though it remains part of Denmark, an EU member state to this day.

Near the Zambezi River, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Botswana and Namibia sit so close together that surveyors still debate whether it forms the world's only true international quadripoint.
The Four Corners Monument in the American Southwest marks the only spot where four US states — Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah — meet at a single point.

Sikkim was an independent Himalayan kingdom until a 1975 referendum, held after Indian troops entered the territory, led to its merger into India as a full state.

Tokelau, a New Zealand territory of about 1,500 people spread across three atolls, has no airport — the only way in or out is a boat from Samoa that can take over a day.
The Cook Islands and Niue both issue their own collector coins and postage stamps, even though everyday transactions run on the New Zealand dollar.
Sri Lanka's official capital is Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte, a suburb of Colombo — but nearly every embassy and business still operates out of Colombo instead.
Switzerland's constitution names no official capital; Bern serves as the seat of the federal government purely by long-standing custom, styled the "federal city.
Israel considers Jerusalem its capital, but for decades most foreign embassies were based in Tel Aviv, reflecting international disagreement over the city's status.
Brazil moved its capital from coastal Rio de Janeiro to the purpose-built city of Brasília in 1960, betting on development of the country's empty interior.
Ivory Coast's official capital, Yamoussoukro, was the birthplace of its first president — yet government offices and embassies remain concentrated in Abidjan.
Washington, D.C. belongs to no US state by design, a deliberate choice meant to stop any single state from wielding outsized influence over the federal government.
Canberra was purpose-built in the early 20th century as a compromise capital after Sydney and Melbourne each refused to concede the honor to the other.
Ottawa became Canada's capital in 1857 partly because Queen Victoria favored an inland site, safer from potential attack along the US border.
Islamabad was built from scratch starting in 1960 to replace Karachi as Pakistan's capital, in part to sit closer to military headquarters in nearby Rawalpindi.
Putrajaya functions as Malaysia's administrative capital, built in the 1990s, while Kuala Lumpur remains the official capital and seat of parliament.
South Tarawa, capital of Kiribati, ranks among the most densely populated strips of land on Earth, even though the entire country has fewer than 120,000 people.
Libya's flag from 1977 to 2011 was a single solid field of green with no design, insignia or text — the only national flag in modern history to be one plain color.
Paraguay's flag is the only national flag with a different emblem on each side: the national seal on the front, the treasury seal on the back.
Denmark's Dannebrog pattern inspired the flags of Sweden, Norway, Finland and Iceland, which all fly variations of the same off-center Scandinavian cross.
New Zealand, Australia, Samoa and Papua New Guinea all place the Southern Cross constellation on their flags, marking their position under southern skies.
Bhutan's flag features a dragon clutching jewels, representing the country's own name for itself, Druk Yul, the "Land of the Thunder Dragon.
Kosovo's flag avoids any single ethnic group's traditional colors, showing instead a gold map of the country beneath six stars for six ethnicities.
Ethiopia's green, yellow and red tricolor, never redesigned under colonial rule, inspired the flag colors of many newly independent African states after 1957.
Somalia's flag carries a single five-pointed star, historically said to represent the five regions where ethnic Somalis lived, including areas now in Ethiopia, Kenya and Djibouti.
The Union Jack combines the crosses of England's St George, Scotland's St Andrew and Ireland's St Patrick, but has never formally included a symbol for Wales.
Canada only adopted its maple leaf flag in 1965, replacing the Red Ensign after a bitterly contested debate in Parliament remembered as the Great Flag Debate.
Portugal's flag carries an armillary sphere, a navigational instrument symbolizing the country's age of maritime exploration.
Colombia, Venezuela and Ecuador all fly variations of the same yellow-blue-red tricolor, a shared legacy of Simón Bolívar's short-lived Gran Colombia.
Rabindranath Tagore wrote the lyrics behind two national anthems, India's and Bangladesh's, and reportedly inspired a third, Sri Lanka's, through one of his students.
Japan's anthem, Kimigayo, pairs some of the oldest lyrics of any national anthem — a poem from around 920 AD — with a melody chosen only in 1880.
Spain, San Marino, Kosovo and Bosnia and Herzegovina are the only four countries whose national anthems officially have no lyrics at all.
Uruguay's national anthem runs roughly five to six minutes in full performance and includes a mid-song solo, reportedly the longest anthem in the world by duration.
Greece and Cyprus share the same national anthem, "Hymn to Liberty," an 1823 poem of 158 stanzas of which only the first two are typically sung.
Tanzania, Zambia and post-apartheid South Africa each built part of their national anthem around the same 19th-century hymn tune, "Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika.
The United Kingdom's "God Save the King" has never been made official by law — it holds its status purely through long-standing tradition.
Liechtenstein's national anthem is set to the exact same melody as the UK's "God Save the King," a tune borrowed by several countries' anthems.
South Africa's national anthem is sung in five different languages within a single song — Xhosa, Zulu, Sesotho, Afrikaans and English — a rare hybrid of two former rival anthems.
Israel's anthem, "Hatikvah," is set to a centuries-old melody with roots in a Sephardic prayer tune that also produced a Romanian folk song and echoes of Smetana's "The Moldau.
Wales sings "Hen Wlad Fy Nhadau" at national sporting events, even though it has no anthem officially recognized separately from the rest of the United Kingdom.
Canada, Australia and New Zealand all used "God Save the Queen" or "the King" as their official or de facto anthem for decades before adopting their own.
India's national anthem has an official short version, lasting well under a minute, distinct from the full multi-stanza version used on formal state occasions.
New Zealand's Chatham Islands run 45 minutes ahead of the mainland, one of only a few places on Earth using a 45-minute time offset.
India and Sri Lanka both keep a single time zone offset by exactly 30 minutes from whole hours, UTC+5:30, despite each spanning wide longitudes.
South Australia and the Northern Territory sit 30 minutes off Eastern Australian time, while the settlement of Eucla, near the WA-SA border, unofficially keeps its own zone 45 minutes off Perth time.
North Korea created its own "Pyongyang Time," UTC+8:30, in 2015 to mark 70 years since liberation from Japan, then abandoned it in 2018 to realign with South Korea.
The Eastern Orthodox churches of Russia, Georgia, Serbia and Jerusalem still follow the older Julian calendar for religious holidays, celebrating Christmas on January 7.
Afghanistan's Solar Hijri calendar counts years from the Prophet Muhammad's migration to Medina in 622 CE but tracks the solar year, keeping it roughly 621 years behind the Gregorian count.
Iran's new year, Nowruz, falls precisely on the spring equinox each year rather than a fixed calendar date, tying the Persian calendar directly to astronomy.
The Hebrew calendar counts years from a traditional creation date around 3761 BCE, keeping its year number more than 3,760 years ahead of the Gregorian calendar's.
China's Lunar New Year shifts against the fixed Gregorian calendar every year because it follows a lunisolar calendar tied to moon phases rather than the solar year alone.
Myanmar uses a 30-minute offset, UTC+6:30, one of just a handful of countries worldwide whose clocks aren't aligned to a whole hour.
Fourteen African countries use the CFA franc, split into two currencies pegged to the euro, a monetary link to France that dates to the colonial era and remains contested today.
Bhutan's ngultrum is pegged one-to-one with the Indian rupee, and Indian rupee notes circulate freely alongside it inside the country.
The East Caribbean dollar is shared by eight island states and territories with separate governments, all pegged to the US dollar at a fixed rate since 1976.
El Salvador adopted the US dollar as legal tender in 2001, then in 2021 became the first country to also make Bitcoin legal tender, before later scaling the policy back.
Kiribati and Tuvalu each mint their own coins for national pride, but both ultimately rely on the Australian dollar as legal tender.
Transnistria, unrecognized by any UN member state, mints and prints its own currency, the Transnistrian ruble, including plastic coins, a rarity in currency production.
North Korea runs two parallel currency systems in practice: an ordinary won of little use to foreigners, and a separate hard-currency system used in hotels and hard-currency shops.
The euro replaced twelve separate national currencies simultaneously in 2002, one of the largest coordinated currency changeovers in modern history.
Turkey dropped six zeros from its lira in 2005, turning one million old lira into a single new lira overnight to combat decades of inflation.
North Korea's 2009 currency redenomination wiped out much of the population's private savings overnight, triggering rare public unrest in a tightly controlled state.
Djibouti has kept its franc pegged to the US dollar since 1949, one of the longest-running fixed exchange rates still in effect anywhere.
Ecuador's currency, the sucre, collapsed so badly in a 1999-2000 crisis that the country dropped it entirely in favor of the US dollar within months.
Many Swiss men keep a government-issued rifle at home after completing compulsory military service, a holdover from the country's citizen-militia defense system.
San Marino did not allow women to run for the office of Captain Regent until 1973, decades after some neighboring countries had already extended similar rights.
Monégasque citizens are barred by law from entering the gaming floor of Monte Carlo's casino, a 19th-century rule meant to keep gambling losses from draining local families.
Bhutan measures national progress with an official "Gross National Happiness" index instead of relying on GDP alone, written into its 2008 constitution.
Longyearbyen's cemetery in Norway's Svalbard archipelago has accepted no new burials since the 1950s — permafrost preserves bodies rather than breaking them down.
The Channel Island of Sark remained Europe's last fully feudal territory until 2008, when it finally held its first democratic elections after over 440 years of rule by a hereditary seigneur.
Under the 1959 Antarctic Treaty, seven countries maintain formal claims to slices of the continent, some overlapping, none internationally recognized as sovereign territory.
A wedge of West Antarctica called Marie Byrd Land, roughly the size of Mongolia, is the largest territory on Earth claimed by no country at all.
Several Antarctic claimant territories issue their own postage stamps, even though the underlying sovereignty claims are effectively frozen under international treaty.
Switzerland's canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden held out against women's suffrage in local elections until 1990, when a federal court finally forced the change.
The Isle of Man and the Channel Islands are Crown Dependencies with their own parliaments and tax systems — not part of the United Kingdom and not in the European Union.
Ladonia, a self-declared micronation inside a Swedish nature reserve, claims tens of thousands of "citizens" worldwide despite covering less than a square kilometre of land.
Copenhagen's Freetown Christiania has operated under its own informally tolerated rules since 1971, including a long-standing open-air cannabis market unlike anywhere else in Denmark.
Singapore bans the sale of chewing gum for non-medical purposes and fines residents for failing to flush public toilets, among the strictest everyday laws in the world.
Bhutan banned all tobacco sales nationwide from 2004 until pandemic-era smuggling concerns forced a partial rollback, one of the strictest tobacco laws on Earth.
Portugal's border with Spain has stayed largely unchanged since a 1297 treaty, making it one of the oldest continuously recognized borders anywhere in the world.

The Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Republic of the Congo are separate countries sharing a border, a river and part of a name — locals distinguish them as Congo-Kinshasa and Congo-Brazzaville.
Niger and Nigeria are two distinct countries named after the same river, though Niger is nearly ten times larger by area and Nigeria has roughly eight times the population.
Guinea, Guinea-Bissau and Equatorial Guinea are three separate African countries that all took their name from the same historic West African coastal region.
Burkina Faso's name, adopted in 1984, blends two local languages into a phrase meaning roughly "land of upright people," chosen to avoid favoring any single ethnic group.
Sri Lanka was known internationally as Ceylon until 1972, when the newly declared republic adopted a name meaning "resplendent island" in Sinhala.
Bangkok's full ceremonial name runs to 169 characters in Thai; most Thais simply call the city Krung Thep, meaning "City of Angels.
A village in Wales carries the 58-letter name Llanfairpwllgwyngyllgogerychwyrndrobwllllantysiliogogogoch, largely extended in the 1860s as a tourism publicity stunt.
A hill in New Zealand's North Island holds an 85-letter Māori name, commonly cited as the longest place name in any English-speaking country.
The French village of Y, population in the dozens, holds one of the shortest place names on Earth at a single letter.
New Mexico's town of Truth or Consequences renamed itself in 1950 to win a radio quiz show promotion, and simply never changed the name back.
Iceland uses patronymic surnames built from a parent's first name rather than inherited family names, so phone directories there are typically sorted by first name.
Cameroon's name traces back to the Portuguese "Rio dos Camarões," meaning "river of shrimp," after explorers noted the abundant shrimp in a coastal estuary.
The Philippines is named after King Philip II of Spain, chosen by a Spanish explorer in 1543, decades before Philip actually took the Spanish throne.
Venezuela's name means "little Venice," reportedly because early explorers thought stilt houses on Lake Maracaibo resembled the canals of the Italian city.
Argentina's name derives from the Latin word for silver, argentum, reflecting early Spanish hopes of finding silver riches in the region.
Brazil is named after pau-brasil, a reddish dyewood tree that was once one of the colony's most valuable exports to Europe.
Ecuador takes its name directly from the equator, which runs through the country roughly 25 km north of its capital, Quito.
Chad, Niger and Mali are all named after major rivers or lakes running through them, a common naming pattern across former French West Africa.
Montenegro's name means "black mountain" in Italian, echoed by the Slavic name Crna Gora, both describing the dark, forested peaks along its coast.
Sierra Leone's name, "Lion Mountains," is traditionally traced to a Portuguese explorer who thought coastal thunder over the hills sounded like a lion's roar.
China and Russia each share land borders with 14 different countries, more than any other nation on Earth, largely a function of their sheer size.
The Canada-US border, including its Alaska segment, runs roughly 8,891 km, the longest international land border between two countries.
The Kazakhstan-Russia border runs about 7,644 km without interruption, the longest continuous land border on Earth, even though the total Canada-US border is longer overall.
Nauru, at about 21 square kilometres, is the world's smallest island nation and the third-smallest country overall, after Vatican City and Monaco.
Tuvalu draws a meaningful share of its government revenue from leasing its ".tv" internet domain to television and streaming companies worldwide.
Andorra's roughly 80,000 residents include a majority who are not Andorran citizens; most hold Spanish or Portuguese nationality instead.
Australia is the only country on Earth that is also an entire continent, and it shares a land border with no other nation.
Indonesia, spread across more than 17,000 islands, shares land borders with only three countries: Malaysia, Papua New Guinea and Timor-Leste.
Tuvalu and Nauru, each with roughly 10,000 to 12,000 residents, rank among the smallest countries by population ever admitted as full United Nations members.
Indonesia has more than 130 active volcanoes within its borders, more than any other country on Earth.
Sweden's own government inventory counted 267,570 islands within its territory in 2013, more than any other country by that measure — most of them uninhabited.
The Maldives has the lowest average elevation of any country on Earth, at only around 1.5 metres above sea level.

Vatican City's crime statistics are sometimes cited as the world's highest per capita — a quirk of dividing pickpocketing cases among 18 million yearly visitors by a resident population of under a thousand.
Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay meet at a single tripoint near Iguazu Falls, one of the few spots on Earth where three countries converge exactly at a river's edge.
The Russia-Norway border runs just under 200 km, one of the shortest frontiers between two large countries, and stayed tightly restricted for ordinary travel until the 1990s.

The 1868 Mannheim Act guarantees landlocked Switzerland free navigation rights on the Rhine, letting barges from Basel reach the sea at Rotterdam — a route still carrying about a tenth of Swiss foreign trade.
Basel's main train station includes a French-run sector, Basel SNCF, with its own platforms under the same roof — a 19th-century treaty arrangement that Schengen-era travelers rarely even notice.
